feedback: If a learner recites fluently from 0 but can't say what comes after 40 in 10s, bring them back to one jump: 'each hop adds ten — show me the next group.'
When the shaded 10s form a single straight column and the 5s two columns, prompt: 'what do you notice about where they are?' so the pattern, not memory, drives the next number.

If a learner sub-counts the in-between numbers under their breath, that is a normal developing step — let the equal jump and the shaded pattern gradually make it feel like one move; do not mark it wrong.
If starting at 30 they restart from 0, say 'start here and keep hopping' and practise entering mid-sequence from several multiples.
activities.intendedInsight: Each step of skip counting adds (or, going back, removes) one equal group, so the next multiple can be predicted from the pattern and from 'one more group' instead of recited — this is the seed of multiplication and repeated addition.
learnerActions: Pick which step size you are counting in: 2, 5 or 10.
Take one step forward on a number line, making an equal-sized jump (a jump of 5 for 5s) that lands on the next multiple.
For each jump, add a GROUP of that many counters into a new stack/tower, so you see the jump as 'one more group of five'.
Shade or light up the cells you land on (5, 10, 15 …) on a hundred square as you go.
Say aloud what each step adds: 'each hop adds five — one more group of five.'
Try starting from a non-zero multiple (e.g. start at 30 and count on in 10s: 30, 40, 50 …).
Try counting in the other direction too (e.g. count back in 10s from 50: 50, 40, 30 …).
activities.title: One hop, one group: linking jumps, counters and the hundred square

feedback: If a learner confuses 'counting in 2s' with 'counting to 2', re-ground in pairs: each new pair adds two to the total.
Use fingers and tally marks to re-establish the fives if the 5s pattern slips.
activities.intendedInsight: Skip counting describes real repeated groups — pairs, fives and tens — so 2s↔even, 5s↔clock/tallies/fingers, 10s↔place value make the counts meaningful and memorable.
learnerActions: Count pairs of objects in 2s and connect to even numbers (2, 4, 6 …).
Count hands/fingers and tally marks in 5s (5, 10, 15 …) and clock minutes in 5s.
Count groups of ten — tens blocks or 10p coins — in 10s and link to place value (how many tens).
Say how each context shows 'one more group': one more pair, one more hand of five, one more ten.
activities.title: Anchoring 2s, 5s and 10s to real things

feedback: A 'next multiple' or 'fill the gap' task checks fluency but, on its own, may let a learner answer by recognition; follow up with 'how did you know?' to check for group reasoning.
In the oral partner game, use the caught slip to prompt 'how did you know that was wrong?' rather than just correcting.
activities.intendedInsight: Repeated varied practice — including continuing from non-zero starts and matching counts to equal-group arrays — builds fluency while keeping the count tied to groups.
learnerActions: Fill in a missing multiple in a sequence (…, 10, __, 20 in 5s).
Say what comes next in 2s/5s/10s from a given number, including across a decade boundary.
Put a set of multiples in order.
Match a skip-count (e.g. 5, 10, 15) to an array or picture of equal groups.
Do an oral count-in-5s with a partner as call-and-response, and catch a deliberate slip in the other person's count.
activities.title: Fluency practice: fill, continue, match
